reference_title: Design and Construction of Continuous Flight Auger Piles

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: The chapter presents advantages and limitations of CFA piles, project and geotechnical conditions favorable or problematic for them, applications on transportation projects (bridge piers and abutments, soundwalls, retaining structures, pile-supported embankments) and examples of typical U.S. costs.
sections.body: The chapter presents advantages and limitations of CFA piles and the project and geotechnical conditions that may be favorable or problematic for them; it illustrates applications on transportation projects, including bridge piers and abutments, soundwalls, earth retaining structures and pile-supported embankments, and ends with examples of typical costs for CFA piles in U.S. construction, useful when considering CFA as an alternative to more traditional foundations. (p. 15)
key_points: Covers advantages, limitations, favorable and unfavorable conditions, applications and costs (p. 15).

sections.title: Background
sections.summary: CFA piles have been used more in private commercial work than in transportation work: simple foundation requirements (many piles in a compact area, Figure 3.1), speed, design-build contracting, noise and vibration limits; against them, owners' quality-control and integrity concerns and bridge demands (uplift, lateral, scour, seismic) needing larger diameters and lengths.
sections.body: CFA piles have been more widely used in private, commercial work in the United States and abroad than in transportation work, for reasons both inherent to the technology and institutional: simple foundation requirements, with many piles in a compact area mainly supporting large concentrated dead loads (Figure 3.1); speed of installation; design-build contracting in private work, with contractors motivated toward speed, economy and innovation; requirements to minimize noise and vibration in populated areas; a reluctance of many owners to use CFA piles because of concerns about quality control and structural integrity; and the typical bridge demands for uplift and lateral capacity, scour and seismic considerations, which require pile diameters and possibly lengths beyond those commonly used with CFA piles in U.S. private work. (pp. 15 to 16)
key_points: Commercial use favored by many piles in a compact area, speed, design-build, noise and vibration limits (p. 15).
Owners' concerns about quality control and structural integrity have limited transportation use (p. 15).
Bridge uplift, lateral, scour and seismic demands require larger diameters and lengths (p. 15).

sections.title: Favorable Geotechnical Conditions
sections.summary: Favorable conditions: medium to very stiff clays (side shear within about 25 m, 80 ft; stable during drilling); cemented sands or weak limestone without undrillable layers (excellent side shear); residual soils; medium dense to dense silty and well-graded sands, especially above groundwater; rock overlain by stiff or cemented deposits that allow installation without excessive flighting.
sections.body: CFA piles generally work well in: (1) medium to very stiff clays, where side shear can provide the needed capacity within about 25 m (80 ft) and the clay is stable during drilling and less subject to mining; (2) cemented sands or weak limestone, if they contain no layers too strong to drill with continuous flight augers; the cuttings need not maintain stability, and the rough sidewall and cast-in-place bond give excellent side shear; (3) residual soils, particularly silty or clayey soils with a small cohesion, where installation is fast and economical (p. 16); (4) medium dense to dense silty sands and well-graded sands, even with some gravel, especially with groundwater deeper than the pile length; (5) rock overlain by stiff or cemented deposits, where significant end bearing on rock can be achieved if the overlying soils allow installation without excessive flighting (lifting of soil on the turning auger like an Archimedes pump); rock directly overlain by strong material or a transitional zone is well suited (p. 17). (pp. 16 to 17)
key_points: Medium to very stiff clays: needed side shear within about 25 m (80 ft); stable during drilling (p. 16).
Cemented sands and weak limestone: excellent side shear if no undrillable layers (p. 16).
Residual soils with small cohesion: fast and economical (p. 16).
Medium dense to dense silty and well-graded sands, especially above groundwater (p. 17).
Rock overlain by stiff or cemented deposits: significant end bearing (p. 17).

sections.title: Unfavorable Geotechnical Conditions
sections.summary: Unfavorable conditions: very soft soils (necks, bulges, downdrag); loose or clean uniform sands under groundwater (mining; DD piles more reliable); voids, water pockets, soft lenses or flowing water; hard strata under soft or loose soil, or sand under stiff clay (Figure 3.2), where flighting and decompression occur; highly variable ground; very hard strata; piles over 30 m (100 ft); deep scour or liquefiable layers.
sections.body: CFA installation can be problematic in: very soft soils, where soft-ground instability produces necks or defects and oversupply of grout (costly) gives bulges that increase downdrag, and volume per unit length is hard to control; loose sands or very clean uniformly graded sands under groundwater, where mining potential is high and control of penetration and grout rates is critical (DD piles are likely more reliable, as they densify loose soil); formations with voids, water pockets, very soft lenses or flowing water (e.g., solution cavities in limestone); hard soil or rock overlain by soft or loose granular soil (Figure 3.2a), where slowed penetration in the hard stratum lets the overburden be flighted by side loading, and decompression and subsidence can occur even with stiff clay under water-bearing sand (p. 17). A hard rock layer under soft material also makes sound bearing hard to assure (piles are driven to resistance; shafts socketed). A sand stratum between two clays also tends to be flighted, with a cone of sand collapsing toward the hole: a void beneath the upper clay, loosened sand and grout over-consumption; driven piles or drilled shafts with casing or slurry are more favorable there (p. 18). Where a clean, dense, water-bearing sand bearing stratum underlies stiff clay (Figure 3.2b), the slow penetration used in the clay loosens and flights the sand, the pile carries almost no tip load and relies on side shear in the clay; better to terminate in the clay or drill into the sand. Also unfavorable: highly variable ground (non-uniform drilling criteria, QC/QA problems, unreliable capacity predictions); very hard strata (avoid penetration, or use socketed shafts or driven piles; CFA piles bearing on hard rock need a smaller bearing value because sound contact is hard to achieve); piles longer than 30 m (100 ft), needing unusually high torque, lifting capacity and tall leads; deep scour or liquefiable layers, giving high bending stresses at depth, which favor larger drilled shafts or driven piles, or steel pipe or H inserts. Applications requiring significant shear, bending or uplift resistance may not suit CFA piles in any soil because of reinforcement limits; groups may serve, but another system may be more economical (p. 19). (pp. 17 to 19)
key_points: Very soft soils: necks, defects, bulges that increase downdrag (p. 17).
Loose or clean uniform sands under groundwater: high mining potential; DD piles likely more reliable (p. 17).
Hard stratum under soft or loose soil: flighting and decompression above it (Figure 3.2a) (p. 17).
Sand between clays: void under the upper clay, loosened sand, grout over-consumption (p. 18).
Sand bearing stratum under stiff clay: tip resistance lost; terminate in the clay or drill into the sand (p. 19).
CFA piles on hard rock need a smaller bearing value; contact hard to assure (p. 19).
Piles longer than 30 m (100 ft) need unusual equipment (p. 19).
Significant shear, bending or uplift demands may not suit CFA piles (p. 19).

sections.title: Project Conditions Affecting the Selection and Use of CFA Piles
sections.summary: Favorable project conditions: speed (300 to 450 m, 1,000 to 1,500 ft, per day on private projects; 60 to 150 m, 200 to 500 ft, on transportation projects); batter piles limited to 1H:4V or steeper; many piles; low headroom; secant or tangent walls up to 10 m (33 ft) exposed with piles under 1.2 m (4 ft); soundwalls; pile-supported embankments.
sections.body: CFA piles may be viable where: speed matters, given a good working platform and favorable ground (Figure 3.3); typical private production for 300 to 450 mm (12 to 18 in.) piles under 20 m (65 ft) long is about 300 to 450 m (1,000 to 1,500 ft) per day, but 60 to 150 m (200 to 500 ft) per day should be expected on transportation projects with spread-out bents or many battered piles; batter piles are required, though speed drops, rig capability is diminished and cages are harder to place with cover; batter should generally be limited to 1 (horizontal):4 (vertical) or steeper for bearing piles, flatter (to horizontal) only for anchor piles in competent non-caving soil; large numbers of piles are required, with prices often a few dollars per foot less than prestressed concrete or steel piles of similar size and capacity (p. 20); low headroom, often more cost effective than high strength micropiles in favorable ground (Figure 3.4), but continuous grouting is impossible when the auger string is broken, so only in favorable ground with close control of pressure and volume; secant or tangent pile walls up to 10 m (33 ft) exposed height with piles under 1.2 m (4 ft) diameter (Figure 3.5), with heavy rigs for vertical alignment, possibly steel sections for reinforcement, higher walls with tiebacks; soundwalls in favorable soil, with many short piles (Figure 3.6); and pile-supported embankments, where per-pile loads are modest and CFA, especially DD, piles may be an effective alternative to ground modification (Figure 3.7), requiring consideration of edge stability, pile caps, the reinforced embankment and the magnitude and rate of settlement (Collin, 2004; Han and Akins, 2004) (pp. 21 to 22). (pp. 20 to 22)
key_points: Private production about 300 to 450 m (1,000 to 1,500 ft) per day for 300 to 450 mm piles (p. 20).
Expect 60 to 150 m (200 to 500 ft) per day on transportation projects (p. 20).
Batter generally limited to 1H:4V or steeper for bearing piles (p. 20).
Low headroom CFA only in favorable ground with close control of grout pressure and volume (p. 21).
Secant or tangent walls up to 10 m (33 ft) exposed height, piles under 1.2 m (4 ft) (p. 21).
Pile-supported embankments: consider edge stability, caps, reinforced fill and settlement (p. 22).

sections.title: Advantages and Limitations of Drilled Displacement Piles
sections.summary: Drilled displacement (DD) piles densify sandy soils and raise horizontal stress (Figure 3.8), giving higher side shear in loose to medium dense sands, less flighting, shorter lengths and little or no spoil; but they need much more torque, are rarely longer than about 20 to 25 m (65 to 80 ft), are not used in rock or hard cemented soils, and displacement can affect nearby structures.
sections.body: DD piles share many features of CFA piles; the differences: better performance in loose sandy soils, as they increase horizontal stress and densify the soil around the pile (Figure 3.8), giving higher side shear in loose to medium dense sands, less flighting, less concern in mixed profiles and a given capacity at a shorter length than a CFA pile of similar diameter; little or no spoil, an advantage where ground is contaminated or spoil must be limited; difficulty penetrating dense or hard soils, because of much greater torque, so DD piles are not installed as deep as CFA piles, lengths over about 20 to 25 m (65 to 80 ft) are not very common, and they are not used in rock, weak rock or hard cemented soils (p. 23); and displacement effects in confined areas or near utilities and sensitive structures, with closely spaced DD piles able to cause large pore pressures in loose fine-grained soils, where partial displacement piles may work better (p. 24). (pp. 23 to 24)
key_points: DD piles densify sands: higher side shear, shorter length for a given capacity (p. 23).
Little or no spoil, useful for contaminated ground (p. 23).
Lengths over about 20 to 25 m (65 to 80 ft) not very common; not used in rock or hard cemented soils (p. 23).
Displacement can affect utilities and structures and raise pore pressures (p. 24).

sections.body: Several typical applications of CFA piles for transportation projects are described: soundwalls (3.4.1), bridge piers and abutments (3.4.2), retaining structures (3.4.3) and pile-supported embankments (3.4.4). (p. 24)
key_points: Applications: soundwalls, bridges, retaining structures, embankments (p. 24).

sections.title: Soundwalls
sections.summary: Soundwall foundations are single piles at each column with reinforcement or anchor bolts for a moment connection (FDOT standard detail, Figure 3.9); lightly loaded, controlled by overturning from wind; typically 450 to 900 mm (18 to 36 in.) diameter and 4 to 8 m (13 to 26 ft) deep. CFA piles are an alternative to drilled shafts.
sections.body: CFA foundations for soundwalls are an easy-to-implement application: single piles at each column with reinforcement or anchor bolts designed for a moment connection to the column (Figure 3.9, the Florida DOT standard detail). The piles are lightly loaded, with design controlled by overturning from wind loads; a typical foundation is 450 to 900 mm (18 to 36 in.) in diameter and 4 to 8 m (13 to 26 ft) deep. CFA piles are an alternative to drilled shafts for these foundations. (pp. 24 to 25)
key_points: Soundwall piles: design controlled by overturning from wind (p. 24).
Typical 450 to 900 mm (18 to 36 in.) diameter, 4 to 8 m (13 to 26 ft) deep (p. 24).

sections.title: Bridge Piers and Abutments
sections.summary: Bridges suited to CFA piles: interchanges (no major scour), approaches, widenings. TxDOT's Krenek Road bridge (64 CFA piles, 450 mm, 17 to 19 m) carried 810 kN (90 tons) design load almost entirely by side friction, with tip resistance near zero from decompression of the bearing sand; CFA piles would have been better ended in the clay. Unit cost about $65/m ($20/ft).
sections.body: Where conditions are favorable, CFA piles are a feasible bridge foundation, most often for interchange structures (where scour is not major), approach structures or widenings, and where driving vibration or noise limits cannot be met or for cost or speed. Few U.S. bridges used them; Vipulanandan et al. (2004) describe TxDOT's Krenek Road bridge in Crosby, Texas (Pleistocene Gulf coast soils), built entirely on CFA piles as an implementation project with load tests to failure and instrumented production piles, about 1 km (0.6 mile) from the Runneburg Road bridge on driven piles in very similar soils (p. 25). The site had stiff clays with two thin sand layers and groundwater about 1.5 m (5 ft) deep; the bridge was founded on 64 CFA piles 17 to 19 m (56 to 62 ft) long and 450 mm (18 in.) in diameter (Figure 3.10), abutment piles on a 1:4 batter, bents on 4-pile groups, designed to terminate in a dense sand stratum (Figure 3.11) with a design axial capacity of 810 kN (90 tons). Runneburg Road used 400 mm (16 in.) square prestressed piles driven to 14 m (46 ft), entirely in the stiff clay, for the same 810 kN (90 tons) mainly by side friction (p. 26). Each vertical CFA pile was installed in about 15 minutes; battered abutment piles took about 45 minutes for each type (one third of that for the driven piles was pre-boring). The contractor had difficulty placing full-length cages (grout viscosity, delays) and was seen turning the auger in the hole without excavating or pumping while waiting for grout, which increased mining in the sand (p. 27). Load tests showed the CFA piles mobilized higher side friction than the driven piles (estimated, as the driven piles were not fully instrumented) and virtually zero base resistance, probably from decompression of the dense sand during drilling through the clay. Twelve instrumented production piles carried the loaded bridge by side friction alone with about 3 mm (0.1 in.) movement (Figure 3.12); the CFA piles would have been better designed to terminate in the clay. CFA unit cost was about $65 per linear meter ($20 per linear foot), about $7 per meter ($2 per foot) above normal because of instrumentation and full-length cages; $1,140 per pile at the central bent. The driven piles cost less, but adjusted to a similar factor of safety the CFA piles would have been about 8% less; TxDOT planned further use where conditions are favorable (p. 28). (pp. 25 to 28)
key_points: Suited to interchange structures (no major scour), approaches and widenings (p. 25).
Krenek Road: 64 CFA piles, 450 mm (18 in.), 17 to 19 m (56 to 62 ft), 810 kN (90 tons) design (p. 26).
Rotating the auger in the hole while waiting for grout increased soil mining (p. 27).
CFA base resistance virtually zero from decompression of the dense bearing sand (p. 28).
Production piles carried the bridge by side friction alone, about 3 mm (0.1 in.) movement (p. 28).
Lesson: terminate in the clay rather than seek end bearing in water-bearing sand below it (p. 28).
CFA unit cost about $65 per linear meter ($20 per linear foot) (p. 28).

sections.title: Retaining Structures
sections.summary: CFA secant or tangent pile walls (cantilever or anchored), usually contractor design-build (Figure 3.13): diameters generally limited to about 1 m (40 in.); depths no more than 10 to 18 m (33 to 60 ft), wall heights generally 12 m (40 ft) or less; verticality critical; secant sequencing with weaker primary and stronger secondary piles (Figures 3.14, 3.15); reinforcement harder to place.
sections.body: CFA piles can form secant or tangent pile walls like drilled shaft walls, designed as cantilever or anchored walls; the vertical element serves as a drilled shaft, slurry wall section or sheet pile would, and the contractor almost always provides the design as a design-build option (Figure 3.13). Differences from other pile types: diameters are generally limited to about 1 m (40 in.); maximum depths are generally no more than 10 to 18 m (33 to 60 ft), with wall heights generally around 12 m (40 ft) or less, because of machine capability, placing reinforcement into fluid concrete and verticality of long piles; verticality control is critical, especially for watertight walls, and hydraulic rigs with inclinometers suit this work; for secant walls the installation sequence and the set time and early strength of the concrete are critical so that previously drilled piles can be cut, some contractors using a weaker mix for primary piles and a stronger mix for the secondary piles that give the wall its main strength (Figures 3.14 and 3.15), with large, high torque rigs (p. 29); and reinforcement placement is more difficult than in a drilled shaft or slurry wall, where it is placed ahead of the concrete (p. 30). (pp. 29 to 30)
key_points: CFA wall pile diameters generally limited to about 1 m (40 in.) (p. 29).
Depths generally no more than 10 to 18 m (33 to 60 ft); wall heights about 12 m (40 ft) or less (p. 29).
Secant walls: weaker primary piles, stronger secondary piles; high torque rigs (p. 29).

sections.title: Pile-Supported Embankments
sections.summary: CFA piles for pile-supported embankments over weak, compressible subsoils can be a cost-effective alternative to ground modification or driven piles where settlement must be limited or construction accelerated: cycle times of 15 minutes or less per pile and costs about $40 per meter ($12 per foot) for 300 to 350 mm piles. Example: Italian railway widening (Figure 3.16).
sections.body: CFA piles for a pile-supported embankment may be a cost-effective alternative to ground modification or driven pile support. Pile support is likely only where the foundation strata are weak, compressible subsoils that would take long to consolidate (p. 30) and post-construction settlement must be minimized or construction accelerated: widening existing embankments, fills for settlement-sensitive facilities (such as high-speed rail) or approach fills to pile-supported structures, and projects where traffic shifts, instrumentation and delays are unacceptable. CFA piles offer speed and economy: cycle times of 15 minutes or less per pile are not uncommon, and costs on the order of $40 per linear meter ($12 per linear foot) are feasible on large projects with many 300 to 350 mm (12 to 14 in.) piles. Figure 3.16 shows a pile-supported embankment for an Italian railway widening, used to limit settlement of the existing railway and new line; the piles were capped with precast concrete-filled cylinder sections (Figure 3.7) and the overlying fill reinforced with geotextiles (p. 31). (pp. 30 to 31)
key_points: Pile support considered for weak, compressible subsoils that would take long to consolidate (p. 30).
Cycle times of 15 minutes or less per pile; about $40 per linear meter ($12 per linear foot) (p. 31).

sections.title: Construction Cost Evaluation
sections.summary: Few U.S. transportation cost records exist. Private projects: about $40 to $60 per meter ($12 to $20 per foot) for 300 to 450 mm piles; transportation projects likely higher. Examples: Texas SH 7 bridge, 760 mm piles at $200 per meter ($60 per foot); Kansas DOT $72 to $85 per meter ($22 to $26 per foot); Florida DOT soundwalls $200 to $260 per meter ($60 to $80 per foot).
sections.body: Because U.S. transportation use has been very limited, cost records are few. Private projects often cost about $40 to $60 per linear meter ($12 to $20 per linear foot) for 300 to 450 mm (12 to 18 in.) piles, but they have larger quantities and fewer moves than a bridge or soundwall, so transportation prices, and performance and integrity testing costs, are likely higher; site constraints on productivity are a major factor, and length, diameter, reinforcement, grout strength, region and project size all affect cost. A Texas bridge on State Highway 7 in Houston County (awarded early 2005) has 24 piles of 760 mm (30 in.) bid at $200 per linear meter ($60 per linear foot) for 237 m (778 ft), plus $25,000 mobilization and $25,000 for each of two static load tests. Kansas DOT used 400 to 450 mm (16 to 18 in.) piles on two bridges and a secant wall at about $72 to $85 per linear meter ($22 to $26 per linear foot), with low headroom work bid at $320 per linear meter ($98 per linear foot); prices are sensitive to mobilization and the number of piles (p. 31). Florida DOT uses CFA piles for soundwalls, usually 760 to 900 mm (30 to 36 in.) and less than 9 m (30 ft) deep, bid at about $200 to $260 per linear meter ($60 to $80 per linear foot), with 6 to 15 piles per day; Frizzi and Vedula (2004) compare CFA with driven precast piles in south Florida (p. 32). (pp. 31 to 32)
key_points: Private projects about $40 to $60 per linear meter ($12 to $20 per linear foot) for 300 to 450 mm piles (p. 31).
Transportation project prices and testing costs likely higher (p. 31).
Texas SH 7: 760 mm (30 in.) piles bid at $200 per linear meter ($60 per linear foot) (p. 31).
Kansas DOT $72 to $85 per linear meter ($22 to $26 per linear foot); fewer piles cost more per foot (p. 31).
Florida DOT soundwalls $200 to $260 per linear meter ($60 to $80 per linear foot), 6 to 15 piles per day (p. 32).
